blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A random variable is a rule that assigns a number to each outcome of an experiment. It is written with a capital letter (X); a particular value it takes is written in lower case (x).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: So far each question was about one event: a positive test, a rolled 4. A random variable packages every numerical result of an experiment, together with its probability, into one object you can calculate with: its average, its spread, its probability of exceeding a threshold.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: X = “number of children, out of 5 tested, who have a positive stool test for worms”. X can be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, each with its own probability. X is the random variable; “X = 3” is one event concerning it.

points.html: Random variables are discrete (a countable set of values, §5.6.1) or continuous (any value in a range, §5.6.2), mirroring the discrete/continuous split of data (recall §1.1.1).
Every random variable has a probability distribution: a complete description of how likely each value, or each range of values, is (§5.7).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A discrete random variable takes a countable set of values x₁, x₂, … , each with probability P(X = x). The list of values and their probabilities is the probability mass function (PMF). Its expected value (mean) and variance are

E(X) = μ = Σ x × P(X = x)

Var(X) = σ² = Σ (x − μ)² × P(X = x).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The PMF is a relative frequency table for the whole population (recall §1.4.3) rather than for a sample. The expected value is the weighted mean of the possible values, each weighted by its probability (recall the weighted mean, §2.2.2): the long-run average of X over many repetitions, the same idea of expected value first met in §3.6.2 as the average over all possible samples. The variance is the probability-weighted average squared deviation from μ, the population variance of §3.6.1 written with probabilities in place of relative frequencies.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
X = number of ANC visits (capped at 4) made by a randomly chosen woman in a block:

x 0 1 2 3 4
P(X = x) 0.05 0.10 0.15 0.30 0.40

The probabilities sum to 1. P(X ≥ 2) = 0.15 + 0.30 + 0.40 = 0.85. E(X) = 0(0.05) + 1(0.10) + 2(0.15) + 3(0.30) + 4(0.40) = 2.9 visits. Var(X) = Σ(x − 2.9)²P(x) = 1.39, so σ = 1.18 visits.

points.html: A PMF’s probabilities are all ≥ 0 and sum to exactly 1 (axioms 1 and 2).
The expected value need not be a possible value: 2.9 visits is not something one woman can make.
The named discrete distributions (Bernoulli, binomial and Poisson) are in §5.7.1.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A continuous random variable can take any value in a range. Its probabilities are given by a probability density function (PDF), a curve f(x) ≥ 0 with total area 1 under it. The probability that X falls between a and b is the area under the curve between a and b.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Haemoglobin or diastolic blood pressure can take infinitely many values in any interval, however narrow. Probability is spread over all of them, so any single exact value gets probability zero. Only ranges get non-zero probability, measured as area. The height of the curve is a density (probability per unit of x), not a probability.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: P(diastolic BP is exactly 80.000… mmHg) = 0. P(diastolic BP is between 78 and 82 mmHg) is the area under the BP density between 78 and 82, a non-zero number.

points.html: P(X = x) = 0 for every single value; so P(X ≤ 80) = P(X < 80) for a continuous variable.
Total area under a PDF = 1, the continuous counterpart of a PMF summing to 1.
Mean and variance are defined as for the discrete case, with the sum replaced by an area (an integral); you will not need to compute them by hand in this book.

blocks.label: Checkpoint 5.5

questions.prompt: Explain why the probability that a continuous random variable takes one exact value is zero, and what you calculate instead.
questions.answer: Probability is spread over infinitely many values in any interval, so a single, infinitely precise value receives none of it. You calculate the probability of a range, as the area under the probability density curve between two points.

questions.prompt: Give one discrete and one continuous random variable from your own clinical work, and justify each classification.
questions.answer: Discrete: number of ANC visits, or number of children with a positive stool test out of 5 (countable values). Continuous: haemoglobin in g/dL, or systolic BP (any value in a range, limited only by the instrument). The test is whether the values are countable steps or points on a continuum.

questions.prompt: For the ANC-visit PMF of §5.6.1, find P(X ≤ 1) and check that E(X) = 2.9.
